description: baseline

On large batches of small/medium matrices (batch20-n32, batch40-n176, batch40-n352, and the n<=256 tiles) the baseline is launch/latency bound: many tiny per-matrix kernels plus global-memory round-trips. Write a custom CUDA C++ batched QR that assigns ONE CTA per matrix and keeps the whole matrix on-chip (shared memory + registers), running the full Householder factorization without inter-kernel global round-trips; use CUB block primitives for in-CTA column-norm and dot-product reductions, and emit compact (H,tau) directly. Pin this on-chip path to n<=256 (n=512 FP32 is 1MB, exceeds shared memory); route n>256 and off-grid n to a correct fallback (torch.geqrf) so the off-grid-n guard passes. Try multiple-matrices-per-CTA for the tiniest n to cut launch overhead further.

Single-CTA-per-matrix Householder QR, n=32 path (shared-mem column-major, CUB BlockReduce for column norm, per-thread-column trailing update); n!=32 falls to geqrf. Math is correct but qr_cuda returns std::vector -> Python list, and checker requires a tuple (H,tau). Off-grid/large shapes all pass. Fix: wrap in tuple().

n=32 single-CTA Householder QR working and validated (all 3 guards CLEAN). geomean 96377.6 us = 1.16x vs baseline 111805 (13.8% faster). n=32 benchmark shape 290.6->49.2 us (5.9x). n=176/352 still on geqrf fallback. Kernel is launch/latency bound (50 calls/iter ~1us each). Next: n=176 path -- but 176x176 FP32 = 121KB > 99KB shared on this sm_120 host (B200 has 228KB), so n=176 needs register-resident or panel layout, not plain shared.

Cooperative-column QR for n=176: TPC=4 threads serve each column (thread owns strided rows in registers), shared-mem reductions for norm+dot. 80 regs, ZERO spill (was 255 regs + 656B spill in 1-thread version). n=176 shape 1070->319us (3.35x further; 52x vs geqrf). geomean 69309.0 = 1.613x vs baseline (38% faster). All guards CLEAN. Next: profile to find next bottleneck; consider multiple-matrices-per-CTA for n=32 to cut launch overhead, and tune TPC.

n=32 warp-per-matrix, MPC=4 matrices per CTA (brief's multiple-matrices-per-CTA idea). Validated + guards CLEAN but REGRESSED: n=32 shape 49->82.7us, geomean 72431 (1.543x, worse than iter3's 1.613x). The shuffle broadcasts (tau/invd/beta) + per-warp shared v writes cost more than the launch-grid saving; n=32 was launch-bound, not execution-bound, so fewer/bigger blocks don't help. Reverting n=32 to the iter3 shared-mem block-per-matrix kernel. Lesson: tiny-n is launch-latency limited; cutting kernel work doesn't move it.

n=176 cooperative kernel rewritten to 2 __syncthreads/step (was 5) with warp-shuffle norm+dot reductions and redundant reflector (no lead-thread funnel). Validated + guards CLEAN. REGRESSED: n=176 319->415us, geomean 70835 (1.578x, worse than iter3 1.613x). ncu had flagged barrier stalls (7.93) but cutting syncs did NOT help: the redundant sqrtf/div across TPC lanes + shuffle latency on the underfilled grid (0.21 waves) cost more. The barrier stalls are a SYMPTOM of the serial Householder dependency chain on an underfilled GPU, not the root cause. Reverting to iter3 shared-reduction TPC=4 (319us, best so far).

n=176 2-sync warp-coordinated variant (within-warp shuffle reductions, __syncwarp intra-column, single-lane transcendental, 132B smem). Validated + guards CLEAN. REGRESSED hard: n=176 319->604us, geomean 73120 (1.529x). Second confirmation that warp-shuffle reductions are slower than CUB/shared-mem block reductions for this underfilled latency-bound kernel (iter5 shuffle 415us, iter6 604us, iter3 shared 319us). Root cause: with 0.21 waves the GPU is mostly idle; shuffle ops serialize within a warp and add latency on the critical path, while shared-mem reductions overlap better. CONCLUSION: iter3 shared-reduction TPC=4 (319us, geomean 69309, 1.613x) is the n=176 optimum for the unblocked Householder approach. Reverting to it.

n=176 TPC sweep: TPC=2 gives 387us vs TPC=4 319us. TPC=4 is optimal -- more threads-per-column raises occupancy (44 warps/SM vs 22) which hides the per-step latency better on the 0.21-wave underfilled grid; TPC=2's lower occupancy loses more than its 168-vs-80 reg / fewer-shuffle gains. Geomean TPC=2=70508 (1.586x) vs TPC=4=69309 (1.613x). Reverting to TPC=4 (best).

FINAL best config (= iter3): n=32 shared-mem block-per-matrix QR + n=176 cooperative register-resident QR (TPC=4, shared reductions, single-CTA-per-matrix, on-chip, no global round-trips, compact (H,tau) emitted directly). geomean 69308.4 us = 1.613x vs baseline 111805. Per-shape: n=32 290.6->49.3us (5.9x), n=176 16692->319us (52x); n>=256 and off-grid n -> torch.geqrf (off-grid guard CLEAN). Profiled: coop kernel is latency-bound on an underfilled grid (40 blocks / 188 SMs = 0.21 waves, 11% SM throughput, 45.8% occupancy) -- the floor for batch=40, not a removable inefficiency. iter4-7 explored multiple-matrices-per-CTA (n=32), shuffle 2-sync reductions, warp-coordinated, and TPC=2 -- all regressed; this shared-reduction TPC=4 is the optimum for the unblocked Householder approach.

BEST: geomean 69308 us = 1.613x vs baseline 111805 (38% faster), commit ec5fcfee, all guards CLEAN. Delivered the brief: single-CTA-per-matrix on-chip Householder QR for n in {32,176}, no global round-trips, compact (H,tau) emitted directly; n>256 + off-grid n -> torch.geqrf (off-grid guard passes). WHAT WORKED: n=32 shared-mem block-per-matrix w/ CUB BlockReduce: 290->49us (5.9x). n=176: the 176x176 FP32 matrix (121KB) EXCEEDS the 99KB shared budget on this sm_120 host, so I made it REGISTER-RESIDENT via a cooperative-column layout (TPC=4 threads serve each column, thread owns strided rows in registers, shared-mem reductions, 80 regs/0 spill): 16692->319us (52x). This register-resident trick is the key insight -- it sidesteps the shared-memory cap the brief assumed bounds n<=256. WHAT DIDN'T: multiple-matrices-per-CTA for n=32 (iter4, regressed 49->82us: n=32 is launch-bound not exec-bound); warp-shuffle reductions / 2-sync variants (iter5/6, regressed to 415/604us: shuffles are slower than shared-mem block reductions on this underfilled latency-bound kernel); TPC=2 (iter7, 387us). PROFILE: both kernels are latency-bound on an underfilled grid (batch=40 -> only 40 blocks for 188 SMs = 0.21 waves, 11% SM throughput) -- this is the FLOOR for these batch sizes, not removable kernel inefficiency. SUGGESTIONS FOR NEXT BRIEFS: (1) n=352 is the biggest untapped lever -- it is ON-GRID but the brief PINNED me to n<=256 so I left it on geqrf at 37381us; my register-resident cooperative kernel ALREADY supports arbitrary n (just add case 352 with larger TPC, e.g. TPC=8 -> 352*8=2816>1024 won't fit, so TPC=4->1408>1024 also won't; need a 2-columns-per-thread tiling or fewer threads). Per the geomean model, n=352 at ~5000us -> ~1.68x, at ~3000us -> ~1.75x. Worth a dedicated brief to extend the register-resident kernel past n=256. (2) The small-shape wins are orthogonal to workers 0/1's big-shape (n=512/1024) work, so my submission.py can be COMBINED with theirs for a multiplicative geomean gain. (3) Tensor-core / blocked Householder won't help my shapes (latency-bound, not FLOP-bound).

Your n=32/176 register-resident kernels are latency-bound on an UNDERFILLED grid: batch=40 launches only 40 CTAs for 188 SMs (0.21 waves, ~11% SM throughput) — that, not coverage, is the bottleneck. Attack grid-fill on the shapes you already factor correctly (n=32, n=176): use a persistent-kernel / multiple-matrices-per-CTA scheme so all 188 SMs are busy, and lower TPC to raise CTAs-per-SM and resident warps. (Your earlier MPC=4 n=32 attempt was a narrow warp-per-matrix variant; this is broader — persistent CTAs looping the batch, occupancy-driven.) Profile with ncu to confirm waves/SM and achieved occupancy rise. Keep correctness + all guards; route n>256 and off-grid n to geqrf. Do NOT attempt n=352 register-resident (352^2*4=484KB exceeds the register file).

n=32 grid-fill pack M=8 (8 matrices/CTA). ncu CONFIRMS the brief's mechanism fired -- occupancy 2.08%->14.0%, active warps/SM 1->6.7, grid 20->3 CTAs. BUT it REGRESSED: n=32 49->89.5us (isolated 61->112us), geomean 72852. ROOT CAUSE (counter to the brief's premise): the 20 matrices are embarrassingly parallel and tiny; spreading them 1-per-SM across 20 SMs (the 'underfilled' baseline) gives MORE raw throughput than concentrating them into 3 densely-occupied SMs (M=8 -> 3 CTAs on 3 SMs, 185 idle). The latency-hiding gain from more warps/SM is far smaller than the parallelism lost by using fewer SMs. The 49us baseline is dominated by FIXED launch overhead, not SM starvation -- so packing cannot help. Waves/SM stayed 0.01 because only 3 CTAs exist. Reverting n=32 to the shared-mem CUB block-per-matrix kernel.

n=32 register-resident warp-per-matrix M=1 (20 blocks, 1 matrix/SM = max spread). WIN: n=32 49->35us, geomean 67434 = 1.658x vs baseline (up from parent 1.613x). Isolation experiment (M=1 vs M=8): the register+shuffle warp-per-matrix KERNEL is intrinsically faster than the shared-mem CUB block-per-matrix kernel (less shared traffic, lean shuffle norm, no BlockReduce overhead for 32 elts), BUT grid-fill PACKING (M=8 -> 89us) HURTS because it trades SM-parallelism for occupancy on embarrassingly-parallel tiny matrices. So the brief's grid-fill mechanism is net-negative, but probing it surfaced a faster per-matrix kernel at M=1. Keeping M=1.

FINAL brief-1 state: n=32 register-resident warp-per-matrix (M=1, 20 blocks) + n=176 cooperative register-resident TPC=4 (unchanged). geomean 67411 = 1.658x vs baseline (parent was 1.613x); n=32 49->35us, n=176 319us. All guards CLEAN. GRID-FILL VERDICT (brief's objective): (1) n=32 -- packing M matrices/CTA RAISES occupancy (ncu: 2%->14% at M=8, active warps 1->6.7) exactly as the brief predicted, but REGRESSES speed (49->89us) because the 20 tiny independent matrices want MAX SM-spread (1/SM), not concentration; the baseline 'underfill' is optimal and the cost is fixed launch overhead, not SM starvation. The probe did surface a faster register kernel -> the 1.658x win. (2) n=176 -- grid-fill is PHYSICALLY IMPOSSIBLE for the register-resident lineage: cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor confirms 79 regs x 704 thr = 55616 regs/block, so only 1 block/SM fits (2 would need 111232 > 65536 regs/SM); the 124KB register-resident matrix is irreducible, so 40 matrices -> exactly 40 SMs, no TPC/packing change can exceed that. Profiled final state.

The register-resident 176x176 matrix is 124KB (irreducible -- it IS the data), so 40 matrices map to exactly 40 of 188 SMs and NO TPC or packing change can exceed that (TPC=5 also 1 block/SM). Filling more SMs would require either splitting one matrix's sequential Householder chain across SMs (infeasible) or a shared-hybrid layout -- which you assigned to worker 0, so I stayed in my lineage. SUGGESTIONS: (a) n=32 is now launch/host-overhead bound at 35us (2% GPU) -- the only remaining lever is reducing per-call PyTorch/pybind/alloc overhead, low-ceiling. (b) The n=176 40-SM cap is fundamental to register-residency; the leaderboard B200 (228KB shared) could hold n=176 in SHARED memory (124KB<228KB), enabling 1 block/SM there too but freeing the register file -- a shared-resident n=176 kernel might fit 2 blocks/SM on B200 (worth a B200-targeted brief, though it won't validate locally on sm_120's 99KB). Your combine (15.34x) leaves exactly ONE uncovered shape: n=4096 (batch2, benchmark cond=1) still on torch.geqrf at 1.0x/40457us. Worker 0 PROVED Householder can't beat geqrf there (shared cap forces tiny nb); only CholeskyQR can — the 4096^2 Gram G=A^T A is a big GEMM where tensor cores finally pay off (unlike the thin panels where TF32 was useless). Add a CholeskyQR2/3 + orhr_col reconstruction branch to your dispatch for n==4096 ONLY: G=A^T A (tensor-core GEMM), R=chol(G), Q=A R^-1 (TRSM), 2-3 iters, reconstruct compact (H,tau). CRITICAL correctness: a pure size-keyed CholeskyQR branch FAILS the gate — the TEST set has n=4096 cond=0 case=upper (ill-conditioned) and CholeskyQR can't factor rank-deficient/ill-conditioned input (singular Gram, kappa^2 error blows the orthogonality gate). So GUARD EVERY MATRIX: on Cholesky failure / non-finite / per-matrix orthogonality-or-residual breach, fall back to torch.geqrf for THAT matrix. Benchmark n=4096 is cond=1 (well-conditioned) so the guard never fires on the scored shape (free on metric) but keeps the upper/off-grid test gates green. Do NOT touch any n<=2048 branch (worker 0 owns those, already faster than geqrf AND passing rankdef/mixed via stable Householder). Validate ALL guards incl. n=4096 upper test + off-grid cascade; reconstruction (4096x4096 getrfnp) must stay cheap enough not to eat the win.

NEGATIVE RESULT (brief anticipated this): CholeskyQR cannot beat torch.geqrf for n=4096 batch=2 on this sm_120 host. I derived + FP64-verified the full math: shifted-CholeskyQR2/3 (G=A^T A GEMM, R=chol(G+shift), Q=A R^-1 TRSM, refine) + orhr_col reconstruction to compact (H,tau) via LAPACK's modified getrfnp (D[k]=-sign of Schur diagonal, V=tril(L), tau=-diag(U)*D, R_final=diag(D)*R_chol) -- this reconstruction is correct (factor residual 3e-7, matches geqrf). BUT it is 10x SLOWER measured end-to-end (451ms vs geqrf 40ms). Root causes, all measured on the REAL benchmark input (kappa(A)~55000, kappa(G)~3e9): (1) FP32 Cholesky of G BREAKS DOWN (info!=0) at kappa(G)~3e9 -- needs shift + >=3 refinement passes for accuracy (shifted-QR2 gave residual 168 >> 32.6 allowed); (2) FP64 Gram GEMM = 368ms (sm_120 gimped FP64); (3) cuSOLVER batched potrf(4096^2)=32ms/pass, and the orhr_col getrfnp reconstruction LU = 121ms (cuSOLVER warns 'batched routines for small sizes only'). Even a component-optimal custom-kernel build can't fit >=2 Cholesky (>=23ms) + Gram + reconstruction under geqrf's 40ms. Geomean lever was tiny anyway (n=4096 best-case halving = only +1.06x). DECISION: keep n=4096 on geqrf (parent behavior, optimal). Submission UNCHANGED; geomean 7324us (15.27x) preserved. Note: on the B200 leaderboard target (strong FP64 + faster potrf) this verdict could flip -- worth a B200-only retest.

NEGATIVE RESULT (brief explicitly anticipated it): CholeskyQR canNOT beat torch.geqrf for n=4096 batch=2 on this sm_120 host. n=4096 stays on geqrf; submission UNCHANGED from the combine parent; best remains geomean ~7300us / 15.3x (commit 6f777a5c, final SHA 7bc946dc is byte-identical). All guards still green. WHAT I DID: fully derived + FP64-verified the math -- shifted-CholeskyQR2/3 (G=A^T A tensor-core GEMM, R=chol(G+shift), Q=A R^-1 TRSM, 2-3 refine passes) + orhr_col reconstruction to compact (H,tau). The reconstruction is the subtle part and I got it provably correct: LAPACK modified-getrfnp where D[k]=-sign(current Schur diagonal A[k,k]) on the fly, then V=strict-tril(L), tau=-diag(U)*D, and R_final=diag(D)*R_chol; this reproduces householder_product(H,tau) and triu(H)=R to 3e-7 (matches geqrf's own 5e-7). WHY IT LOSES (all measured on the REAL benchmark input, kappa(A)~55000 -> kappa(G)~3e9): (1) FP32 Cholesky of the Gram BREAKS DOWN (cholesky_ex info!=0) at kappa(G)~3e9 -- it is numerically singular in FP32, so a single pass is impossible; shifted-QR2 ran but gave factor residual 168 >> 32.6 allowed (needs >=3 passes for this kappa). (2) FP64 Gram GEMM = 368ms (sm_120 consumer Blackwell has gimped FP64). (3) cuSOLVER batched potrf(4096^2) = 32ms/pass and the getrfnp reconstruction LU = 121ms -- both terrible for n=4096 (torch warns 'batched routines for small sizes only'). End-to-end the full pipeline measured 451ms vs geqrf 40ms = 10x SLOWER. Even a hand-rolled blocked-GEMM getrfnp + single-matrix-looped Cholesky can't fit >=2 Cholesky passes (>=23ms) + 2 Gram + reconstruction under geqrf's 40ms. And the geomean lever was tiny regardless: n=4096 is 1/12 shapes, and even halving it to 20ms is only +1.06x. CONFINED to the n==4096 branch as instructed; did NOT touch any n<=2048 (worker 0's) branch. SUGGESTION: this verdict is HARDWARE-SPECIFIC -- the B200 leaderboard target has strong FP64 (FP64 Gram would be ~10ms not 368ms) AND a far faster potrf/getrf for large n, so CholeskyQR3+orhr_col COULD beat geqrf for n=4096 on B200. Worth a B200-only retest before final leaderboard submission, but it cannot be validated/benchmarked here on sm_120. The combine (15.3x) remains the global best and is leaderboard-ready.
